documents.name: optimizers.md
sections: Gradient descent is the basic way neural networks learn. The loss function measures how wrong the predictions are, and its gradient points in the direction of steepest increase. Each update moves the weights a small step in the opposite direction: new weight equals old weight minus the learning rate times the gradient. If the learning rate is too large the loss oscillates or diverges; if it is too small, training crawls and may stall on plateaus. Plotting the loss curve over iterations is the simplest way to see which of the two problems you have.

Computing the gradient on the whole dataset for every update is expensive, so practitioners use stochastic gradient descent: each update uses a single example or, more commonly, a mini-batch of 32 to 512 examples drawn at random. The estimate is noisy, but the noise is cheap and even helps escape sharp minima. Batch size interacts with the learning rate: when the batch is doubled, the learning rate is often increased as well. Shuffling the data every epoch keeps the mini-batches representative.

Momentum keeps a running average of past gradients, a velocity, and moves the weights along that velocity instead of the raw gradient. Directions that agree across steps build up speed, while directions that flip sign cancel out, which damps the zig-zag pattern in narrow valleys of the loss surface. A momentum coefficient of 0.9 is the usual default. Nesterov momentum looks ahead by evaluating the gradient at the position the velocity is about to reach, which often converges slightly faster.

Adam combines momentum with per-parameter adaptive step sizes. It tracks an exponential moving average of the gradient (the first moment) and of the squared gradient (the second moment), corrects both for their bias at the start, and divides the first by the square root of the second. Parameters with consistently large gradients therefore take smaller steps. Typical settings are beta1 0.9, beta2 0.999 and epsilon 1e-8. AdamW decouples weight decay from this update, which usually generalises better than adding L2 to the loss.

A fixed learning rate is rarely optimal for the whole run. Schedules change it over time: step decay divides it by ten at chosen epochs, cosine annealing lowers it smoothly towards zero, and one-cycle policies raise it and then lower it. Large models are often trained with warmup, where the rate starts very small and grows linearly over the first few thousand steps before the main schedule begins; this avoids unstable early updates while the adaptive statistics of the optimizer are still poor estimates.

Overfitting happens when a model memorises noise and quirks of the training set instead of patterns that generalise, so training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises. Remedies include collecting more data, data augmentation, L2 weight decay that penalises large weights, dropout that randomly zeroes activations during training, and early stopping, which keeps the checkpoint with the best validation score. A held-out test set that is never used for tuning gives the honest final estimate.

documents.name: transformers.md
sections: Self-attention lets every token in a sequence look at every other token. Each token is projected into a query, a key and a value vector. The attention weight between two tokens is the dot product of one token's query with the other's key, scaled by the square root of the key dimension and normalised with a softmax across the sequence. The output for a token is the weighted sum of all value vectors. Because every pair is compared, the cost grows with the square of the sequence length.

Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel, each with its own learned projections of smaller dimension. One head may track syntax, another long-range references, another nearby words. The heads' outputs are concatenated and projected back to the model dimension. Using eight or more heads costs about the same as one full-width head but gives the layer several different views of the sequence at once.

Attention by itself ignores word order: shuffling the tokens would give the same outputs. Positional encoding fixes this by adding information about each token's position to its embedding. The original transformer used fixed sinusoidal functions of different frequencies; many later models learn position embeddings, and recent ones use rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which rotate query and key vectors by an angle that depends on position so that attention scores depend on relative distance.

An encoder reads the whole input with bidirectional attention and is used for understanding tasks such as classification. A decoder generates text one token at a time and uses a causal mask: each position may attend only to earlier positions, never to tokens that come later, so the model cannot cheat by looking at the answer. Encoder-decoder models such as the original translation transformer combine both, with cross-attention from the decoder to the encoder outputs. GPT-style chat models are decoder-only.

Models do not see characters or whole words but tokens produced by a tokenizer. Byte-pair encoding starts from single bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new symbol until the vocabulary reaches a target size, often 32 to 150 thousand entries. Common words become one token while rare words are split into several subword pieces, so any text can be represented without unknown words. Token counts, not words, determine context limits and cost.

Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model to a task with additional training on task data. Full fine-tuning updates every weight and needs a lot of memory. Parameter-efficient methods train far fewer parameters: LoRA freezes the original weights and learns two small low-rank matrices per adapted layer whose product is added to the frozen weight. QLoRA does the same on top of a 4-bit quantised base model. The resulting adapter is a few megabytes and can be merged or swapped.

documents.name: containers.md
sections: A Docker image is a read-only template: a filesystem snapshot plus metadata such as the default command and environment variables. A container is a running instance of an image with its own writable layer, process space and network interface. Many containers can start from the same image. Stopping a container keeps its writable layer until the container is removed; removing it deletes everything that was written inside it.

A Dockerfile builds an image step by step, and each instruction creates a layer. Docker caches layers and reuses them when the instruction and its inputs have not changed, but once one layer changes every following layer is rebuilt. That is why the order matters: copy the dependency manifest and install dependencies first, and copy the frequently edited source code last. Otherwise every small code edit invalidates the cache and reinstalls all packages, making builds slow.

Data written inside a container disappears when the container is removed. Volumes are the way to persist it: a named volume is managed by Docker and survives container deletion, and a bind mount maps a host directory into the container. Databases should always store their data directory on a volume. Volumes can be backed up by mounting them into a temporary container and archiving their contents.

Containers get their own network namespace. To reach a service inside a container from the host, publish its port: the option -p 8080:80 forwards host port 8080 to container port 80. Containers on the same user-defined bridge network can reach each other by container name through Docker's built-in DNS, without publishing ports. Binding a published port to 127.0.0.1 keeps it reachable only from the host itself.

Docker Compose describes a multi-container application in one YAML file: services, their images or build contexts, environment variables, ports, volumes and networks. One command starts the whole stack with dependencies in order, and another stops and removes it. Compose is ideal for local development and small single-host deployments, for example a web app, its database and a cache defined side by side.

Kubernetes runs containers across a cluster of machines. The smallest unit is a pod, one or more containers sharing a network address. A Deployment keeps a chosen number of identical pods running and replaces them during rolling updates. Services give pods a stable address and load-balance between them. For periodic jobs Kubernetes offers CronJobs, which start a pod on a cron schedule, run it to completion and keep a history of recent runs.

documents.name: databases.md
sections: Most relational databases implement indexes as B-trees: balanced trees whose sorted keys let the database find a value in a logarithmic number of steps instead of scanning every row. An index on a column speeds up lookups, range queries and sorting on that column, but every insert, update and delete must also update the index, so indexes cost write speed and disk space. Index the columns that appear in frequent WHERE clauses and joins, not every column.

A composite index covers several columns in a fixed order, such as last name then first name. It can serve queries that filter on a leftmost prefix of its columns, the first column alone or the first and second together, but not a query that filters only on the second column. A covering index contains every column a query needs, so the database can answer from the index without reading the table rows at all.

A transaction groups several statements so that they succeed or fail as a unit. The ACID properties describe the guarantees: atomicity means all-or-nothing, so a failure halfway rolls back every change; consistency means constraints hold before and after; isolation controls how concurrent transactions see each other; durability means committed data survives a crash, usually thanks to a write-ahead log flushed to disk before the commit returns.

Isolation levels trade correctness for concurrency. Read uncommitted allows dirty reads of other transactions' unfinished changes. Read committed only shows committed data but a repeated read may return a different value. Repeatable read keeps rows stable within a transaction but may allow phantom rows. Serializable behaves as if transactions ran one after another and is the safest but slowest. Many databases default to read committed.

Normalisation organises tables to avoid redundancy and update anomalies. First normal form requires atomic values without repeating groups; second removes partial dependencies on part of a composite key; third removes dependencies between non-key columns. Highly normalised schemas need more joins, so read-heavy systems sometimes denormalise deliberately, storing derived or duplicated data to save work at query time.

Before optimising a slow query, look at its execution plan. EXPLAIN shows how the database intends to run the query: which indexes it will use, the join order and method, and estimated row counts. EXPLAIN ANALYZE in PostgreSQL actually executes it and reports real timings per step. A sequential scan over a large table where you expected an index lookup usually means a missing or unusable index.

documents.name: android-background.md
sections: WorkManager is the recommended Android library for deferrable, guaranteed background work. You describe the work as a Worker or CoroutineWorker, build a request and enqueue it; WorkManager stores the request in its own database, so it survives app restarts and device reboots, and runs it when its constraints are met. Unique work names prevent duplicates: enqueueing again with the same name can keep, replace or append to the existing work.

Constraints tell WorkManager when work may run: a network connection of a given type, for example unmetered for Wi-Fi only, the device charging, the battery not low, storage not low or the device idle. Work waits until all of its constraints are satisfied. When work fails it can return retry, and the backoff policy, linear or exponential with a starting delay, decides when it is attempted again.

Periodic work repeats at an interval of at least fifteen minutes, which is the minimum WorkManager allows. The exact moment is not guaranteed: the system batches work from many apps to save battery, so a job requested every day may run some time after the scheduled point. An initial delay can align the first run with a preferred time of day, but later runs drift. Unique periodic work with the update policy changes an existing schedule without creating a second one.

Doze mode and App Standby restrict background activity to save battery. When the phone is stationary, unplugged and the screen is off, Doze defers jobs, syncs and network access to periodic maintenance windows. App Standby buckets limit how often rarely used apps may run work. Some manufacturers add their own aggressive battery savers, so background work can be delayed for hours unless the user exempts the app from battery optimisation.

A foreground service performs work the user notices and must show an ongoing notification. Since Android 14 every foreground service declares a type, such as dataSync, mediaPlayback or location, and holds the matching permission. Apps cannot start foreground services from the background in most cases. WorkManager can run a long worker as a foreground service via setForeground, which is useful for large uploads or downloads.

Exact alarms fire at a precise time even in Doze, but they drain the battery and require the SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM or USE_EXACT_ALARM permission on recent Android versions. They are meant for user-facing timing such as alarm clocks and calendar reminders. For maintenance tasks like backups or syncing, inexact scheduling with WorkManager is the appropriate choice because the exact minute does not matter.
